column1: # Phase 1 tally. Fill in as you work; nothing here is document text.
# TIMING - minutes per page, one row per page.
# Alternate the order rather than doing one whole set then the other.
page
# ratio = (mean minutes on mt pages) / (mean minutes on scratch pages)
# At or above 1.0 the drafting is not paying for itself.
# EDIT CLASSES - one tick per edit made to a draft. Rough counts are enough.
# The ratio says whether to proceed. This says whether a poor ratio is
# fixable, and they are different questions. A 1.1 driven by terminology is
# nearly free to fix -- there is no glossary yet, so that is the expected
# shape of a first run. The same 1.1 driven by register means every sentence
# needs rewriting, which no configuration solves.
class
ocr
column3: The draft was wrong because the OCR was wrong, not the translation. Count these separately or the ratio blames the model for Tesseract. On an all-scanned corpus this is the row to watch

column1: terminology
column3: Right meaning, wrong term. Fixed by one glossary entry, forever

column1: register
column3: Accurate but reads wrong for a court document

column1: numbers
column3: A figure, date or case number altered or dropped. tr-lint should have caught these - if you are finding them by eye, say so

column1: additions
column3: Words in the translation with no counterpart in the source, e.g. a statutory provision completed from memory

column1: omission
column3: Something in the source missing from the translation

column1: formatting
column3: Merged paragraphs, lost emphasis, table cells shifted

column1: other
column3: Anything that fits none of the above - describe it

column1: # WORTH NOTING SEPARATELY
# - Any draft you abandoned and retranslated from scratch, and why.
# - Anything the draft got right that you expected it to get wrong.
# - Whether the bilingual layout helped or got in the way.
# IF EVERY SOURCE IS A SCAN
# Then the comparison is not really "machine translation against none". It is
# "OCR plus machine translation against reading the page yourself", and both
# halves of that can fail. The ocr row above is what separates them.
# A poor ratio driven by the ocr row is not a verdict on translation. It says
# the text going in is damaged, and the fixes live upstream: better scanning,
# different OCR settings, or a second OCR engine cross-checking the first.
# That cross-check exists and has been run on real scans: tools/ocr-check.py
# reads the same pages with Tesseract and deepseek-ocr:3b and compares the
# numbers. Over eight pages of two scanned documents the two engines agreed
# on every number on seven of them, and disagreed on fourteen on the eighth
# -- which was also the page Tesseract itself was least sure of. It costs
# about 3 minutes a page, so --gate runs it only where Tesseract's own
# confidence is low.
# Also worth timing, separately from translation: how long it takes to read
# an OCR text layer against its page and correct it. On an all-scanned corpus
# that cost is paid on every page whether or not any machine translation
# happens, so it belongs in the quote either way.
